reply: The first step is to treat the new blend as a separate sample set: use the existing NIR probe to collect spectra and build a fresh calibration against an independent reference assay, and in parallel acquire Raman spectra (e.g., with a 785 nm probe) to evaluate whether the Raman data add useful orthogonal information. This experiment will tell if the NIR model can be transferred or must be rebuilt and whether Raman is worth adding.

risks: Matrix change may alter NIR scattering/absorption enough to require a new calibration.
Raman signal may be weak in highly scattering powders, requiring longer integration or higher laser power.
Probe fouling or dust buildup could affect signal stability; cleaning procedures must be defined.

steps: Prepare a set of representative powder samples covering the expected API concentration range of the new blend.
Simultaneously acquire Raman spectra with a 785 nm probe on the same samples.
Obtain reference API concentrations using the agreed reference method (e.g., HPLC).
Build an NIR calibration model (e.g., PLS) and evaluate its prediction error.
Build a Raman‑only model and a fused NIR‑Raman model to assess any improvement.
Validate each model on held‑out samples not used in calibration.
Measure each sample with the existing NIR probe in the same in‑line geometry used for the current process.
feasibility.decisionBasis: If the NIR model meets the agreed error criteria, the existing calibration can be updated without Raman. If Raman (alone or fused) reduces error or improves robustness, consider adding Raman for production monitoring. Agree two things separately with the customer before the test: the model accuracy required against the reference method, and the alarm or action threshold applied to the measured value.
